young.html: In the Timaeus, a thinker named Timaeus tells the story of how the world was made. He says it is only a “likely story,” the best guess he can give. In his story, a good and wise maker, whom he calls the Craftsman, looked at a perfect pattern and shaped the world to be as good and beautiful as it could be.

Timaeus says everything is made of four elements: fire, air, water and earth. And each element is made of tiny shapes! Fire is made of little pyramids with 4 triangle faces, which is why fire is sharp and stings. Air is made of shapes with 8 faces, water of shapes with 20, and earth of little cubes, which is why earth is solid and stays put.

young.name: gb-elements
young.cap: Break water into air and fire, or join fire into air, and count the triangles.

young.html: Build Plato's fire. Draw a large triangle with three equal sides on stiff paper. Mark the middle of each side and join the marks, making four small triangles. Cut out the big triangle, fold along the lines, and tape the three corners together at the top. That is a tetrahedron, Plato's shape for fire. If you have more time, try eight triangles for air (an octahedron).

The book also tells, for the first time anywhere, the story of Atlantis, a mighty island kingdom beyond the Strait of Gibraltar that tried to conquer the Mediterranean and then sank into the sea in a single day and night. People have searched for Atlantis for centuries. Most scholars think Plato invented it to tell a story about pride and good government.

full.html: The Timaeus and its unfinished sequel, the Critias, were written late in Plato's life, about 360 BC. They are set the day after Socrates described an ideal city (much like the Republic's). Now his friends repay him: Critias will tell a story of that city in action, and first Timaeus, from the Greek city of Locri in southern Italy and an expert on astronomy, will describe the making of the world up to the creation of human beings.
Critias says that Solon, the Athenian lawgiver, heard from Egyptian priests at Sais that ancient Athens, nine thousand years before, had defeated a great power from the Atlantic:

full.text: The most famous of them all was the overthrow of the island of Atlantis. This great island lay over against the Pillars of Heracles, in extent greater than Libya and Asia put together, and was the passage to other islands and to a great ocean of which the Mediterranean sea was only the harbour…
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press

full.html: “The Pillars of Heracles” are the rocks at the Strait of Gibraltar; “Libya and Asia” meant North Africa and what is now Turkey and the lands east. The Critias describes Atlantis, ringed with canals, grown proud and greedy, and breaks off just as the gods meet to judge it.

Taking Atlantis as history. It appears nowhere before Plato, no ancient remains have been found, and the story serves Plato's themes. Most scholars treat it as a story Plato made up, though many have proposed real places that might have inspired it.
Timaeus says that the world, which we know only through the changing senses, can be described only by a likely account, not with the certainty of mathematics. Then he begins:

full.text: Let me tell you then why the creator made this world of generation. He was good, and the good can never have any jealousy of anything. And being free from jealousy, he desired that all things should be as like himself as they could be.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press

full.html: In Timaeus's account, the Craftsman (Greek dēmiourgos) does not make things from nothing: he brings order to a moving, disorderly chaos, looking to an eternal pattern. The world is a single living being with a soul, round like a sphere, the most perfect shape. Its soul is laid out according to musical ratios, and its circles carry the stars and planets.

full.text: Wherefore he resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and when he set in order the heaven, he made this image eternal but moving according to number, while eternity itself rests in unity; and this image we call time.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press

full.html: Time came with the heavens. For Timaeus, there were no days, months or years until the heavens moved. The sun, moon and planets were made to mark and measure time.

Timaeus builds the four elements from two kinds of right triangle, assembled into regular solids (the shapes Euclid proves, in his last book, are the only five). Fire is the tetrahedron, sharp and light; air the octahedron; water the icosahedron, round enough to flow; earth the cube, the steadiest. The fifth solid, the dodecahedron, he says the god used for the whole.

full.name: gb-elements
full.cap: Fire, air and water share the same equilateral faces, so they can change into one another. Earth cannot.

full.title: Trading triangles
full.q: Timaeus says a particle of water can break into two of air and one of fire. Check the face count, and work out how many fire particles come from 3 particles of air.
steps: Water (icosahedron): 20 faces. Air (octahedron): 8 faces. Fire (tetrahedron): 4 faces.
Each air particle has 8 faces, enough for $8 \div 4 = 2$ fire particles.
So 3 air particles make $3 \times 2 = 6$ fire particles.

full.html: Later parts describe the human body: the head is round like the cosmos, the eyes send out a gentle fire that meets daylight, and illness comes from the elements getting out of balance.

The Timaeus presents Plato's own picture of the world's making, through Timaeus, as a likely story. Different religious traditions have their own accounts of creation; this lesson reports Plato's, without judging any of them.

deep.text: A long life in later books

deep.html: For many centuries, the Timaeus was almost the only work of Plato that scholars in western Europe could read, in a partial Latin translation by Calcidius. Medieval thinkers compared its Craftsman with the creation in Genesis, and discussed how far the two agreed. Kepler, later on this ladder, tried to fit the planets' orbits between Plato's five solids. The question “why is nature mathematical?” runs from the Timaeus through Galileo and Newton.

Aristotle, in On the Heavens, criticized the idea that elements are made of flat triangles, and argued that the world had no beginning. Modern chemistry kept the idea that matter is made of small building blocks with shapes, but found more than four elements and no triangles.

items: Why might Timaeus call his account only a “likely story”? Is that true of scientific theories today?
Did time begin, or has it always been?
Why do people keep looking for Atlantis, even when it is probably a story?

questions: Timaeus thought fire was made of tiny pyramids because fire is sharp. What shape would you give to water, or to ice? Why?
What is the difference between a story and a theory? Can a story teach something true?
Why do you think the Atlantis story became so famous?
Timaeus says the maker of the world was good and wanted everything to be good. What do you think makes a world good?
Time is “a moving image of eternity.” What do you think that means?
